idiom_name: consumer-owned port interface + adapter struct + explicit DTO conversion (the package boundary is the ACL)
implementation_notes: Go makes the boundary a package: the consumer declares the small interface it needs (type OrderPort interface { Place(ctx context.Context, o Order) (Receipt, error) }), the adapter package owns the DTO structs with `json:"..."` tags, the http.Client and the conversion functions (func toLegacy(o Order) legacyOrder), while encoding/json and errors.Is/As do the mechanical half. What replaces the facade/adapter/translator object trio is the unexported conversion function plus the consumer-side interface; embedding the vendor client is the wrong shortcut because it promotes the vendor's whole method set back into the domain's view. The explicit adapter struct is still justified when the port has several methods or the client needs configuration; for a single call, one struct with one method is the same boundary.
pitfalls: Embedding the vendor client promotes its whole method set, so callers start calling the upstream directly through the adapter - the leak the layer exists to prevent.
ctx must be threaded through every call; a context.Background() inside the adapter silently disables the caller's cancellation and deadlines.
Untyped error passthrough (returning the vendor's *url.Error or status) re-imports the upstream vocabulary; wrap into your own sentinel errors and translate with errors.Is.
Interfaces are satisfied implicitly, so nothing forces the port to live with the consumer: declaring it next to the vendor inverts the dependency direction.
